shocks.title: United States 50 percent tariffs on selected Canadian goods

facts.label: In force since
facts.value: 19 August 2026

facts.label: Coverage
facts.value: 554 tariff lines, three proclamations

facts.label: Scale
facts.value: Roughly 5 percent of Canadian goods exports to the US

facts.label: CUSMA exempt
facts.value: No

shocks.plain: The United States has put a 50 percent tax on about one twentieth of what Canada sells them. Most trade is not on this list. It does cover hockey equipment, furniture, clothing, wine and beer, dairy, cement, plywood, circuit boards and some vehicles. If your workplace ships any of those south, this is the week to ask your employer what it means for orders.
shocks.operator: Effective 12:01am on 19 August 2026 across 554 tariff subheadings in three proclamations. The United States importer of record pays the duty, so the pressure arrives as cancelled orders and price renegotiation rather than as a bill to you. Qualifying under CUSMA does not exempt these lines, which catches most people out. Stop quoting a US landed cost without it, and check your Incoterms to confirm who actually carries the duty.
shocks.policy: First use in history of Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, which permits up to 50 percent against a country found to have discriminated against United States commerce, requires no investigation and carries no expiry. Three proclamations: 52 subheadings covering dairy and agriculture, 439 covering motor vehicles and diverse manufactured and agricultural goods, and 63 covering alcohol, wood, paper and hockey equipment. Chapter 99 headings 9903.03.12 to 9903.03.14 carry the 50 percent rate; 9903.03.15 and 9903.03.16 list carve-outs at zero. Goods already under Section 232 are generally excluded. Legal challenge is widely expected given the statute has no judicial precedent.

shocks.title: Canada's matching counter-tariffs

facts.label: Announced
facts.value: 22 August 2026

facts.label: Comes into force
facts.value: 8 September 2026

facts.label: Instrument
facts.value: Product list and rates published 25 August 2026, updated 26 August (27.6 billion dollars of US imports)

facts.label: Approach
facts.value: 15, 25 or 50 percent, matching the US rate line for line

shocks.plain: Canada is answering with its own taxes on American goods, starting Tuesday 8 September, the day after Labour Day. The list was published 25 August: steel, dairy, appliances, farm equipment, paper, electronics and more, covering 27.6 billion dollars of what Canada buys from the US. Each product gets matched to whatever rate the US is charging on the equivalent Canadian good, so some items carry 15 percent, some 25, some 50.
shocks.operator: The product list and rate schedule were published 25 August 2026 and updated 26 August, covering 27.6 billion dollars of US imports at 15, 25 or 50 percent depending on the good, mirroring the US rate on the matching line. If you import from the United States, 8 September is the date that changes your landed cost, not 19 August. Named sectors are steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics. Check your own HS codes against the published list now rather than waiting for the formal surtax order and CBSA customs notice, which will formalize what has already been announced.
shocks.policy: Announced by the Prime Minister on 22 August 2026 following suspension of negotiations. The Department of Finance published the product list and rate structure on 25 August 2026, updated 26 August, setting three tariff rates of 15, 25 and 50 percent, with each product's rate matching what the United States charges on the equivalent Canadian good, covering 27.6 billion dollars of US imports. The formal surtax order in Canada Gazette Part II and the CBSA customs notice giving declaration detail were not yet located as of this check on 27 August 2026 and should still be confirmed against the Department of Finance list in the meantime.

shocks.title: Federal support package for affected workers and businesses

facts.label: Size
facts.value: 7.5 billion dollars in new measures announced 25 August 2026, on top of nearly 25 billion dollars delivered over the prior 18 months

facts.label: Announced
facts.value: 22 August 2026

facts.label: Program detail
facts.value: Published 25 Aug 2026: Regional Tariff Response Initiative (1.5B), BDC Pivot to Grow (500M), Canada Strong Diversification Fund (2B), Rapid Response Supports for Workers and Employers (3.5B), and expanded flexibility on the existing 10B Large Enterprise Tariff Loan Facility

shocks.plain: The federal government has now published exactly what it is doing to help workers and businesses hurt by these tariffs: an extra 7.5 billion dollars announced 25 August, on top of nearly 25 billion dollars already put into support programs over the past year and a half. It covers loans and grants for affected businesses, extra help for large employers under strain, and better Employment Insurance for people who are laid off or have their hours cut. If your hours are cut, ask your employer about Work-Sharing and the expanded EI measures, since those are the two programs built to keep people on payroll or afloat between jobs.
shocks.operator: Announced 25 August 2026 as 7.5 billion dollars in new and enhanced measures, layered on nearly 25 billion dollars the government says it has delivered over the prior 18 months. The five pieces: the Regional Tariff Response Initiative (1.5 billion, higher per-SME funding caps), the BDC Pivot to Grow program (500 million in new working-capital loans of 250,000 to 5 million dollars), the Canada Strong Diversification Fund (2 billion, a new Strategic Response Fund stream), Rapid Response Supports for Workers and Employers (3.5 billion, including waived EI waiting periods, expanded benefits and a Workforce Retention and Retraining Program), and expanded flexibility on the existing 10 billion dollar Large Enterprise Tariff Loan Facility (up to 36 months of liquidity support, 15-year maximum terms). Application windows for the newer pieces are still opening; have your last two years of financials, your US revenue concentration and your affected headcount ready.
shocks.policy: Announced 25 August 2026 as 7.5 billion dollars in new and enhanced measures, on top of nearly 25 billion dollars in supports the government says it has delivered over the prior 18 months, including the earlier 1 billion dollar Business Development Bank of Canada program and 500 million dollars in additional Regional Tariff Response Initiative funding announced in May 2026, delivered through the regional development agencies. Delivery agents and full eligibility criteria for each new stream were still being rolled out as of this check on 27 August 2026. Earlier working notes in this project carried unsourced figures for a national support envelope; those should be discarded in favour of this one.

shocks.title: Canadian surtax on United States steel and aluminum

facts.label: Rate
facts.value: 25 percent of the value for duty

facts.label: In force since
facts.value: 13 March 2025

facts.label: Instrument
facts.value: SOR/2025-95, last amended 1 September 2025

facts.label: Remission
facts.value: Steel Derivative Goods Surtax Remission Order exists

facts.label: Rate from 8 September 2026
facts.value: 50 percent of the value for duty, under the same order

shocks.plain: Canada has had its own tax on American steel and aluminum since March 2025, well before this month. It is 25 percent, it is still in place, and it is part of why building materials have been getting more expensive. From 8 September 2026 that charge doubles to 50 percent.
shocks.operator: A 25 percent surtax on US-origin steel and aluminum, in force since 13 March 2025 and separate from anything happening in September. It already sits in your landed cost. The schedule of covered goods was replaced on 1 September 2025, so a list you saved before that date is out of date. A remission framework exists for steel derivative goods, so if you are paying surtax on inputs with no Canadian substitute, that is worth raising with your broker. Goods marked as originating in Puerto Rico, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, American Samoa or the US Virgin Islands are outside the order. Finance Canada's published counter-tariff list confirms that steel and aluminum goods already carrying the 25 percent surtax move to 50 percent on 8 September 2026, under this same order rather than a new one. Price anything landing on or after that date at the higher rate, and check your classifications against the published list rather than against a schedule you saved earlier.
shocks.policy: United States Surtax Order (Steel and Aluminum 2025), SOR/2025-95, registered 12 March 2025 and effective 13 March 2025, imposing 25 percent of the value for duty on US-origin goods in the listed classifications. Amended 27 March 2025, 8 April 2025, and 1 September 2025, the last of which replaced Schedule 1 with Schedule 2. Not repealed. Note that the consolidated text on the Justice Laws site is current only to 17 June 2026, so an amendment made after that date would not yet appear there and should be checked against the CBSA customs notices. Finance Canada's complete list of US products subject to counter-tariffs, published 25 August 2026 and updated 26 August, increases the rate on the steel and aluminum goods already covered by this order from 25 to 50 percent effective 8 September 2026. The increase runs under this order, SOR/2025-95, rather than a separate instrument.

shocks.title: Global safeguard on imported cabinets and vanities

facts.label: Rate
facts.value: 25 percent of the value for duty

facts.label: In force since
facts.value: 31 July 2026, provisional for up to 200 days

facts.label: Not applicable to
facts.value: Canada, United States, Mexico, Chile, Israel and CIFTA beneficiaries, developing countries

facts.label: Tribunal inquiry due
facts.value: by 15 January 2027

shocks.plain: Kitchen cabinets and bathroom vanities brought into Canada from most countries carry an extra 25 percent charge. Cabinets made in Canada, the United States or Mexico are not affected. This has nothing to do with the argument with the United States, and it is temporary while a tribunal decides whether to make it permanent.
shocks.operator: A provisional safeguard surtax of 25 percent of the value for duty on certain wood cabinets and vanities and their subassemblies, including flat-pack, in force from 31 July 2026 for up to 200 days. It does not apply to goods originating in Canada, the United States, Mexico, Chile, Israel or another CIFTA beneficiary, or in developing countries. If you are sourcing cabinets from the United States or Mexico this does not touch your cost. If you are sourcing from elsewhere in Asia or Europe it very likely does, and it is a live line in a renovation quote alongside the steel and aluminum surtax. Classification of a subassembly is not obvious here, so confirm it with your broker rather than assuming.
shocks.policy: Certain Wood Cabinet and Vanity Goods Surtax Order, effective 31 July 2026, imposing 25 percent of the value for duty as a provisional safeguard for a period of up to 200 days while the Canadian International Trade Tribunal conducts a global safeguard inquiry. The Tribunal inquiry is expected to conclude by 15 January 2027 and the provisional measure ceases if no injury to domestic producers is found. The exclusions follow Canada's trade obligations rather than being discretionary, which is why the United States and Mexico are outside it. This is a domestic trade remedy and not a counter-measure, and treating it as part of the United States dispute misreads it.

shocks.title: Trade negotiations suspended

facts.label: Negotiators recalled
facts.value: 21 August 2026

facts.label: Next formal talks
facts.value: None scheduled

shocks.plain: Canada walked away from a deal rather than sign one it judged bad. That means there is no quick fix coming and no date to wait for. Plan on this lasting.
shocks.operator: There is no near-term settlement to hold out for, so treat the current cost structure as the working assumption for at least the next two quarters rather than as a temporary spike to absorb. That changes the calculation on repricing, on qualifying an alternate supplier, and on whether to renew a US-dependent contract at current terms.
shocks.policy: Negotiations suspended on the evening of 21 August 2026 and negotiators recalled to Ottawa, with the Prime Minister citing terms described as uneconomic and unfair and demands that would have constrained Canada's ability to conclude other trade agreements. Sovereignty, protection of the French language and culture were stated as never having been on the table. The stated alternative track is domestic building and diversification, including more than twenty trade and security agreements signed in the past year, tariff-free access to 1.5 billion consumers with an intent to double that within six months through ASEAN and India, and European Union discussions opening this autumn.
